title: Huntsville Cold Case Unit Closes Two 2010 Homicides, Names Dead Suspect - NewsBreak
text:
By admin ,
12 hours ago
The Huntsville Police Department’s Cold Case Unit has closed two Huntsville cold case homicides from 2010 after investigators linked a man who died in 2013 to both killings.
Police said 15 years of unanswered questions ended when investigators established probable cause that Jeremy Powell killed 60-year-old Herbert Gray in July 2010 and 41-year-old Eden Arlene Lua in November 2010. Powell died in 2013, so neither case will go to prosecution.
Powell was a suspect from the start
HPD’s Major Crimes Unit first investigated both deaths, which police ruled homicides. Detectives considered Powell a suspect in each case but could not build enough evidence to establish probable cause at the time.
Powell knew Gray. He also lived near Lua when she was killed, according to HPD.
TV interview and fingerprints
The Cold Case Unit kept working through evidence and information from both investigations. Investigators found a television news interview with Powell recorded shortly after Lua’s death. Police said statements he made in it led them to look harder at his possible role in the killings.
Investigators also learned that Powell moved to Mississippi soon after Lua died. In April 2013, a Jackson Police Department investigator questioned him about an unrelated homicide. Powell shot the investigator to death and then killed himself, according to HPD.
HPD investigators later got Powell’s fingerprints from the Jackson Police Department. They compared those prints with evidence from the Gray investigation. The prints matched ones recovered at the homicide scene and inside Gray’s vehicle, which someone stole after his death.
District attorney review
Investigators took their findings to the Madison County District Attorney’s Office for review. Based on the evidence, probable cause was established linking Powell to both homicides. HPD closed both investigations.
“These families have waited more than 15 years for answers about what happened to their loved ones,” HPD Chief Kirk Giles said. “The passage of time does not diminish our commitment to victims and their families. I’m grateful for the dedication of our investigators and their continued efforts to find answers.”
The Cold Case Unit continues to review unsolved cases, pursue new leads and reexamine evidence for victims’ families, police said.
